evidence.claim: The White Mountain Trail makes a 100-mile driving loop through mountain passes and sections of the White Mountain National Forest.
evidence.quote: The Trail is a loop tour that winds through sections of the 800,000-acre White Mountain National Forest

evidence.claim: White Mountains Attractions Association presents this National Scenic Byway as a route joining mountain scenery, historic landmarks and recreation.
evidence.quote: The White Mountains have long been known for natural splendor, cultural richness, historical charm, and stimulating recreation well as some of the most beautiful scenery in the eastern United States. The White Mountains Trail, designated a National Scenic Byway, encompasses all these aspects throughout its 100-mile route.

evidence.claim: In Franconia Notch, the parkway narrows to one lane in each direction between Cannon Mountain and Mount Lafayette.
evidence.quote: Dominated by Cannon Mountain to the west and Mount Lafayette to the east, it lies principally within Franconia Notch State Park and is traversed by the Franconia Notch Parkway (Interstate 93 and U.S. Route 3). The parkway required a special act of Congress to sidestep design standards for the Interstate highway system because it is only one lane in each direction.

evidence.claim: The crossings had practical work to do before they became a scenic circuit. In 1803, the Tenth New Hampshire Turnpike was extended through Crawford Notch to Lancaster.
evidence.quote: The Tenth New Hampshire Turnpike from Portsmouth was extended through the notch to Lancaster in 1803.

evidence.claim: The turnpike and the later Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad gave settlers northwest of the mountains a route through Conway toward coastal trading ports.
evidence.quote: The turnpike and later Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad through Crawford Notch opened a new route through the White Mountains for settlers of the area to the northwest to reach Conway on the way to the trading ports on the coast.

evidence.claim: The Crawford family built trails and kept inns in the notch during the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: It was named for the Crawford family, who were trail-builders and hostelers there in the 19th century.

evidence.claim: Sylvester Marsh’s railway climbs by engaging a toothed wheel with a ladder-like rack with open rungs.
evidence.quote: The rack rail design used is one of Marsh's own inventions, using a ladder-like rack with open bar rungs engaged by the teeth of the cog wheel.

evidence.claim: It was the world’s first mountain-climbing cog railway.
evidence.quote: The Mount Washington Cog Railway, also known as the Cog, is the world's first mountain-climbing cog railway (rack-and-pinion railway).

evidence.claim: Marsh obtained his charter in 1858, but the Civil War delayed work until 1866.
evidence.quote: Marsh obtained a charter for the road on June 25, 1858, but the American Civil War prevented any action until May 1866.

evidence.claim: Paying passengers rode the unfinished line in August 1868; construction reached the summit in July 1869.
evidence.quote: Despite the railroad's incomplete state, the first paying customers started riding on August 14, 1868, and the construction reached the summit in July 1869.

evidence.claim: The base road leaves US 302 at Bretton Woods.
evidence.quote: Just off Rte. 302 in Bretton Woods is the Mt. Washington Cog Railway (base road entrance 27.8)

evidence.claim: On the railway, a locomotive pushes a single passenger car uphill and reverses for the descent.
evidence.quote: Each train consists of a locomotive pushing a single passenger car up the mountain, descending the mountain by going in reverse.

evidence.quote: The notch is traversed by U.S. Route 302, which closely follows the Saco River southeast to North Conway

evidence.claim: In August 1826, Samuel Willey’s family and two hired men died in a landslide here.
evidence.quote: the site of the historic Willey Slide (34.6), where the Willey family of seven and two hired men died in a 1826 landslide.

evidence.claim: They had left their house for a shelter; the slide destroyed the shelter while leaving the house untouched.
evidence.quote: They fled their home and took refuge in a shelter, but it was destroyed while the house remained unscathed.

evidence.claim: An uphill rock outcrop split the slide, which passed on either side of the house and reunited below it.
evidence.quote: A rock outcrop uphill divided the slide, which flowed around the home and reunited below it.

evidence.claim: The house later became part of a larger inn and burned in 1898.
evidence.quote: The house became part of a larger inn, then burned in 1898.

evidence.claim: Mount Willey, on the notch’s western side, bears the family’s name.
evidence.quote: Mount Willey, on the west side of the notch, is named in their memory.

evidence.claim: The loop’s Kancamagus connection came much later: two dead-end roads were joined in August 1959.
evidence.quote: The Kancamagus Highway opened in August 1959, after two dead-end stretches of road were linked, creating a connection between US 3 in Lincoln and NH 16 in Conway.

evidence.claim: Paving followed in 1964, and the first winter plowing came in 1966–67.
evidence.quote: the road was paved in 1964, and in the winter of 1966–67 it was plowed for the first time.

evidence.quote: Later designs introduced horizontal boilers, slanted so that they remain close to horizontal on the steeply graded track.
